intro: Read the deck for the evidence and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, gives you a way to remember it and warns where practitioners slip. Work the section exercises in pencil, answer the recall questions aloud, and run your own programme through the 5 Rs checklist as you go.

sections.title: What the Care Economy Is
sections.big_idea: Care is **the economy beneath the economy**: paid and unpaid work that sustains people, and the precondition of all other production.
in_plain_words: The care economy covers cooking, cleaning, fetching water and fuel, looking after children, the sick and the elderly, and the paid work of domestic workers, nurses, teachers and frontline workers. Direct care (feeding a child, nursing) and indirect care (cooking, water) both count. Unpaid care is not counted in GDP, and the paid side is underpaid, so both halves form a single subject.

The circuit of social reproduction explains why: care produces people, people supply labour, markets produce output, and output funds services and care. When public services contract, the work returns to households and then to women. The ILO estimates 16.4 billion hours of unpaid care a day, **76% of them done by women**. Reframe care spending as investment.

diagram.caption: when the last link fails, care returns to women

key_terms.meaning: Paid and unpaid activity that meets people's physical, emotional and developmental needs.
Care of a person: feeding, nursing, supervising.
Housework and water and fuel that make direct care possible.
Care produces workers, markets use them, output funds care.
A frontline worker paid a fixed sum and classed as a volunteer.
Whether care spending is booked as consumption or as human capital.

worked_example.title: Unpack the ILO 2018 figures
worked_example.setup: The ILO estimates 16.4 billion hours of unpaid care work a day worldwide, 76% of it done by women.
steps: Hours done by women: 16.4 × 0.76 = 12.46 billion.
Hours done by men: 16.4 − 12.46 = 3.94 billion.
Ratio of women's to men's hours: 12.46 ÷ 3.94 = 3.16, which matches the deck's 3.2 times.
People needed to do 16.4 billion hours at 8 a day: 16.4 ÷ 8 = 2.05 billion.
worked_example.answer: About 12.46 billion hours by women, a ratio of roughly 3.2 to 1, and the equivalent of 2 billion people working 8 hours unpaid.

mistakes: Treating paid and unpaid care as two separate subjects.
Quoting a care figure without its source, year and method.
Calling honorarium workers volunteers without noting the dispute about the classification.
Booking childcare and eldercare as pure cost in appraisal.

recall.q: Which care activities does the deck class as indirect?
recall.a: Cooking and washing up, cleaning, fetching water and firewood, shopping and household management.

recall.q: Which care activity does GDP not count?
recall.a: Unpaid domestic work and unpaid care of children and elders at home.

recall.q: What are the steps in the circuit of social reproduction?
recall.a: Care produces people, people supply labour, markets generate output, and output funds services and care.

recall.q: What share of global unpaid care hours do women do, per the ILO?
Why does the deck say infrastructure changes policy traction?
recall.a: Cooking and water can be reduced by services and infrastructure instead of being redistributed between people.

sections.title: The Invisibility of Care
sections.big_idea: GDP counts goods and services that are **bought and sold**, so the same work is visible when paid and invisible when unpaid.
in_plain_words: The System of National Accounts draws a production boundary. Unpaid production of goods for own use, such as subsistence farming, is inside it, while unpaid services such as cooking, cleaning and caring are outside. The boundary follows whether money changed hands, a measurement convention. The housekeeper paradox shows the arbitrariness: GDP falls when a paid housekeeper becomes an unpaid spouse doing the same work.

Care was naturalised as love and instinct, so it was denied the status of labour. Feminist economists such as Waring, Folbre, Elson and Razavi named the gap. Invisible care means no budget line and designs that assume it is free. **Satellite accounts** now value household production beside GDP, using time-use surveys.

diagram.caption: goods count, services within the home do not

key_terms.meaning: Gross Domestic Product: goods and services bought and sold.
System of National Accounts, the UN rulebook for GDP.
The line deciding which activities count as economic production.
A parallel estimate valuing household production alongside GDP.
Treating care as instinct and love so it is not seen as skilled labour.
An input no design process asks about, so its supply is assumed unlimited.

worked_example.title: Inside or outside the boundary?
worked_example.setup: Classify six activities under the SNA as the deck describes it.
steps: Growing food for your own household: inside (own-account production of goods).
Cooking it for your own household: outside (unpaid domestic service).
The same meal in a restaurant: inside (market production).
Fetching water for the household: inside the SNA boundary, though seldom recorded.
Caring for an elderly parent at home: outside (unpaid care of household members).
The note: the boundary follows money, a convention and no economic judgement.
worked_example.answer: Inside: farming food, the restaurant meal, water. Outside: cooking at home, caring for the parent.

mistakes: Treating the boundary as an economic finding when it is a convention.
Reading rising GDP from commercialised services as more work being done.
Assuming 'women appear not working' means they are available for a programme.
Designing without a budget line because care is assumed to happen for free.

recall.q: What does the housekeeper paradox show?
recall.a: GDP falls when paid work becomes unpaid, though the work is unchanged, which exposes the boundary as arbitrary.

recall.q: Which feminist economist wrote If Women Counted (1988)?
recall.a: Marilyn Waring.

recall.q: Who built the Recognise, Reduce, Redistribute framework?
recall.a: Diane Elson.

recall.q: What is a satellite account?
recall.a: A parallel estimate that values household production alongside GDP without changing the headline number.

recall.q: What is the cheapest correction for invisibility in a programme?
recall.a: Add two time-use questions to a baseline.

sections.title: Measuring Care: Time-Use Surveys
sections.big_idea: A time-use survey records **a full day in slots**, which is how unpaid care finally gets counted, and by whom.
in_plain_words: India's NSO ran its first national Time Use Survey from January to December 2019 and a second round in 2024, with results released in February 2025. Households recount the previous day, activities are coded in 30-minute slots and classified into paid work, unpaid care, learning, leisure and rest. Secondary activity records simultaneous care, which roughly doubles the care total.

The gap is large and consistent: women do many times more unpaid care than men, in rural and urban settings and across states, and thin infrastructure adds hours for women while men's barely move. Proxy reporting, recall bias and the missing mental load mean a reported gap is a lower bound. **Read the tables for your own state** before designing a schedule.

diagram.caption: how the survey records a day

key_terms.meaning: A survey asking people to account for how they spent a full day.
A second activity at the same time, such as minding a child while cooking.
One person reporting for the whole household.
The planning, remembering and worrying that fills no diary slot.
Too little time left for rest, learning, paid work or leisure.
A figure likely to understate the true amount.

worked_example.title: Read a coded day
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A time-use diary uses 30-minute slots. One woman's day shows 10 slots of unpaid care as the main activity, and one man's shows 1.
steps: Slots in a full day: 24 × 2 = 48.
Her unpaid care minutes: 10 × 30 = 300.
In hours: 300 ÷ 60 = 5.
His unpaid care minutes: 1 × 30 = 30.
Check the convention: if a secondary activity is also recorded, the care total roughly doubles.
worked_example.answer: 5 hours for her and 30 minutes for him, on a main-activity-only convention. Always check the convention used.

mistakes: Citing a time-use figure without naming the round or the convention.
Comparing the 2019 and 2024 rounds without reading how the instrument changed.
Accepting proxy-reported data as the real division of labour.
Reading the survey as capturing the mental load.

recall.q: When was India's first national Time Use Survey conducted?
recall.a: January to December 2019, by the NSO.

recall.q: What recording unit does the survey use?
recall.a: 30-minute slots across a 24-hour recall.

recall.q: Why is proxy reporting the largest hazard?
recall.a: The reported division of labour then reflects the norm and misses the actual day.

recall.q: What happens to the care gap where infrastructure is thin?
recall.a: Women's unpaid hours climb further and men's barely move.

recall.q: What can time-use evidence support at design?
recall.a: Childcare investment, leave policy, infrastructure priorities, satellite accounts and programme timing.

sections.title: The Value of Unpaid Care
sections.big_idea: Valuing care means **imputing a wage**, and each choice moves the total. Report the method and give a range.
in_plain_words: Imputation estimates a money value for work with no market price, usually by asking what the equivalent work would cost to buy. Generalist replacement uses a domestic worker's wage and gives a lower estimate. Specialist replacement uses a nurse, cook or tutor per task and gives a higher one. Opportunity cost uses the carer's forgone wage and varies with who she is.

Across countries, valuations typically land between roughly 10% and 60% of GDP, and the spread follows from the method. Comparing care with named industries is vivid but invites a methodological fight. Monetising makes care visible to ministries, yet flattens relationships, anchors to low wages and invites cost-cutting. **Value care to argue for investment, and keep the hours in view.**

diagram.caption: three methods, three scales of answer

key_terms.meaning: Estimating a monetary value for an activity with no market price.
What the equivalent paid work would cost.
The wage the carer forgoes by doing care.
Time when care overlaps another activity; valuing it can double totals.
Pricing care at low care wages, which are low because care is undervalued.
Reporting a spread of values instead of one figure.

worked_example.title: Same hours, two methods
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A woman does 5 hours of unpaid care a day. Assume a generalist wage of Rs 60 an hour and a specialist wage of Rs 120.
steps: Hours a year: 5 × 365 = 1,825.
Generalist replacement: 1,825 × 60 = 109,500 rupees.
Specialist replacement: 1,825 × 120 = 219,000 rupees.
Report both with the method, as a range.
worked_example.answer: Rs 109,500 to Rs 219,000 a year: the method alone doubles the value.

mistakes: Quoting one confident figure without the method.
Treating the spread between estimates as disagreement about the facts.
Assuming valuing care pays the carer anything.
Using 'bigger than manufacturing' without readiness for a method challenge.

recall.q: What does generalist replacement cost use?
recall.a: The wage of a domestic worker, giving a lower estimate.

recall.q: What property of opportunity cost is uncomfortable?
recall.a: An hour of care by a well-paid woman is valued above the same hour by a poor one.

recall.q: What range of GDP share do valuations typically fall in?
recall.a: Roughly 10% to 60%, depending on method and country.

recall.q: Name two limits of monetising care.
recall.a: Any two of: flattens the relational core, anchors to low wages, invites cost-cutting, one number replaces the analysis.

recall.q: What is the deck's balance principle?
recall.a: Count it, but don't reduce it: use valuation to win recognition while insisting care's worth exceeds its price.

sections.title: The Gendered Division of Care
sections.big_idea: Care falls on women and girls through **norms that every institution reinforces**, so single-point interventions disappoint.
in_plain_words: Worldwide, women spend 3.2 times as much time on unpaid care as men, with ratios from 1.7 to 4.7 across regions. Girls are drawn into care early, which costs study time and risks dropout, while boys acquire no care skills. Time poverty results, and a person can be income-poor and time-poor at once, so cash does not buy time back where services do not exist.

The second shift means paid work adds to the day and replaces none of it. Heavier care load goes with lower participation, in both directions of cause. Caste, poverty, rurality, disability and migration stack, and the mental load never occupies a slot. **Disaggregate care data by at least two axes**, and check the evidence on each consequence.

key_terms.meaning: The assignment of unpaid care to women and girls by norm.
Too little discretionary time after unavoidable unpaid work.
Hochschild's phrase for unpaid work after paid work.
Paid work added on top of unpaid work.
The managerial, cognitive work of care.
Held in place by many institutions, each assuming the others enforce it.

worked_example.title: Turn a ratio into a share
worked_example.setup: Worldwide, women spend 3.2 times as much time on unpaid care as men. What share of unpaid care time is theirs?
steps: Let men's time be 1 and women's 3.2.
Total time: 3.2 + 1 = 4.2.
Women's share: 3.2 ÷ 4.2 = 0.76.
That matches the ILO figure of 76% of unpaid care hours.
Regional range: 1.7 to 4.7 times, so the share changes by region.
worked_example.answer: Women do about 76% of unpaid care hours, consistent with the ILO's figure.

mistakes: Reading the care gap as a regional cultural quirk.
Treating a cash transfer as enough where services do not exist to buy time.
Using a single national care average to describe all women.
Counting a shared task as a shared load.

recall.q: How many times more unpaid care do women do than men worldwide?
recall.a: 3.2 times, from 1.7 in the Americas to 4.7 in the Arab States.

recall.q: What did Hochschild name?
recall.a: The second shift of cooking, cleaning and caring after paid work.

recall.q: What does the care-versus-participation chart not establish?
recall.a: Which causes which, or that care alone explains it.

recall.q: Which intersections add to the care load?
recall.a: Poverty, rurality, caste, disability in the household and migration of adults.

recall.q: Why can the mental load not be seen in a diary?
recall.a: It is cognitive and continuous, so it fills no slot.

sections.title: Care & the Macroeconomy
sections.big_idea: The market economy depends on care. **Care investment is infrastructure** and pays back through jobs and women's time.
in_plain_words: Social reproduction is the daily and generational work of producing and maintaining people. The paid economy draws on it for workers and rarely pays back. When demands outstrip resources, carers deplete, which is an economic risk as well as a personal one. Treating care as investment in human capital changes how a budget line is appraised.

Razavi's care diamond shows four providers: state, market, family and community. When state and market do little, the family corner, in practice women, absorbs the rest. Moving care between corners is a distributional decision. Care spending is labour-intensive, creates many jobs for women, frees other women to work and keeps spending in the domestic economy. **Name which corner you shift care to, and who pays.**

key_terms.meaning: Work of producing and maintaining people that replenishes the labour force.
Harm that accumulates when care demands outstrip resources.
Razavi's four providers: state, market, family, community.
Care treated as an investment like a road or power line.
More jobs per unit of spending than capital-intensive options.
Spending that stays in the domestic economy.

worked_example.title: Audit a programme with the diamond
worked_example.setup: A village programme depends on an anganwadi worker, a private crèche, a daughter-in-law and a self-help group.
steps: The anganwadi worker is the state corner. The limit is coverage and quality.
The private crèche is the market corner. The limit is affordability.
The daughter-in-law is the family corner. The limit is depletion.
The self-help group is the community corner. It is often unpaid women's work under another name.
Ask who pays and who does the work in each corner.
worked_example.answer: State, market, family, community. The family and community corners are carried by unpaid women and may be depleting.

mistakes: Crediting community provision as a solution without checking who does the work.
Adding a committee, a new log or a meeting for carers without counting the extra demand.
Booking childcare as consumption and then wondering why it is first to be cut.
Treating the family corner as a choice, when it is the residual.

recall.q: Who proposed the care diamond and when?
recall.a: Shahra Razavi, UNRISD, 2007.

recall.q: What happens when state and market do little?
recall.a: The family corner, in practice women, absorbs the rest.

recall.q: What is depletion?
recall.a: Harm that accumulates when care demands outstrip the resources of carers.

recall.q: Why is care spending effective stimulus?
recall.a: It is labour-intensive, jobs go largely to women, it frees other women's time and has low import content.

recall.q: What are the four things to shift care toward?
recall.a: The state, the market, men within families, and the community.

sections.title: The 5 Rs Framework
sections.big_idea: **Recognise, Reduce, Redistribute, Represent, Reward**: use them together, in sequence, and test any programme against them.
in_plain_words: Elson's three Rs are Recognise (measure and count care), Reduce (cut drudgery with water, fuel, electricity and transport) and Redistribute (move care from women to men and to the state). The ILO added Represent (voice for carers) and Reward (decent pay and protection). Each R has a typical instrument and a typical nominal failure.

They build on one another: recognition comes first, reduction is cheaper than redistribution, and reward without representation rarely sticks. Most national care policies stop after the second R, so the gender share barely moves. As a checklist, ask whether your data captures unpaid care, whether you cut drudgery, who carries the care you assume, whether carers have a say and whether care workers are paid. **Most designs fail the third question.**

diagram.caption: Elson's three Rs plus the ILO's two

key_terms.meaning: Make unpaid care visible and count it.
Cut drudgery through infrastructure and technology.
Shift care from women to men and to the state and market.
Give carers and care workers voice.
Pay and protect paid care workers decently.
Leave that is lost if unused, which raises take-up by fathers.

worked_example.title: Run a programme through the five questions
worked_example.setup: A nutrition programme asks about employment, calls infrastructure someone else's sector, relies on volunteers, 'consulted the community' and pays an honorarium.
steps: Recognise: 'We ask about employment' fails. Add two time-use questions to the baseline.
Reduce: 'That is infrastructure, outside our sector' fails. Treat water, fuel and transport as in scope.
Redistribute: 'Volunteers' fails, and it is the question that makes the others academic.
Represent: 'We consulted the community' fails unless carers can change the design.
Reward: 'They receive an honorarium' fails. Pay carers properly.
worked_example.answer: All five questions fail; Redistribute is the first to fix, with a budget line for the care the programme assumes.

mistakes: Treating recognition as the whole agenda.
Reducing drudgery without redistributing, so the share stays unchanged.
Counting consultation as representation when carers have no authority.
Paying honoraria instead of wages and calling it reward.

recall.q: Which Rs did Elson propose and which did the ILO add?
recall.a: Elson: Recognise, Reduce, Redistribute. ILO: Represent and Reward.

recall.q: What is the clearest test across all five Rs?
recall.a: Which Rs have a budget line, and how large it is relative to the claim.

recall.q: What is the instrument with the best evidence for shifting the within-household share?
recall.a: Non-transferable paternity or parental leave.

recall.q: What is the limit of Reduce?
recall.a: It does not touch the share, and released hours may be absorbed by other unpaid work.

recall.q: Why do most national care policies leave the gender share unchanged?
recall.a: They stop after the second R.

sections.title: Care Policies
sections.big_idea: Care policy is the set of public actions that serve the five Rs: **services, leave, transfers and regulation**. Map each to an R to find the gaps.
in_plain_words: ECCE does double duty only if quality and staffing are adequate and hours match a working day. Anganwadis under ICDS are care infrastructure already in place, run by a worker who carries nutrition, pre-school, health and reporting. India's 26 weeks of paid maternity leave covers mainly the formal sector and attaches to mothers, so it does not redistribute.

Eldercare is the crisis arriving fastest, and social protection such as pensions and maternity benefit is care policy by another name. Strong care systems abroad, such as the Nordic ones, show a policy choice and need adapting. **Ask four questions of any policy**: does it reduce unpaid work, redistribute care, avoid being tied to formal employment and fund the care workforce.

key_terms.meaning: Early Childhood Care and Education for children under six.
Integrated Child Development Services, delivered through anganwadi centres.
Raised paid maternity leave to 26 weeks in the organised sector.
Pensions and transfers that fund care without being labelled care.
Whether a policy relies on unpaid or honorarium workers.
Part of leave reserved for fathers that is lost if unused.

worked_example.title: Check the hours condition
worked_example.setup: A village offers an ECCE centre open 3 hours a day, and mothers in paid work have an 8-hour day. A formal-sector mother is entitled to 26 weeks of leave.
steps: Working day uncovered by the centre: 8 − 3 = 5 hours.
The centre helps the child but does not enable paid work, however good it is.
Maternity leave in days: 26 × 7 = 182.
Who is covered? Organised-sector employees only, a small minority of working women.
Who is left out? Informal workers, and fathers have no comparable entitlement.
worked_example.answer: 5 hours of the working day are uncovered, and 182 days of leave reach only formal-sector mothers.

mistakes: Counting a short-hours centre as enabling paid work.
Expanding anganwadi duties without costing the worker's time.
Designing entitlements around formal employment in an informal economy.
Copying a Nordic model wholesale instead of adapting its direction.

recall.q: Which R does childcare and ECCE mainly serve?
recall.a: Redistribute.

recall.q: How many weeks of paid maternity leave did the 2017 Act provide?
recall.a: 26 weeks, for eligible women in the organised sector.

recall.q: What is the transferable lesson from the Nordic systems?
recall.a: Making part of leave non-transferable, a low-cost design change with well-documented effects.

recall.q: Which question is decisive in South Asia?
recall.a: Whether the policy is tied to formal employment, which excludes most women.

recall.q: What does a policy delivered by volunteers do?
recall.a: It transfers cost instead of funding care.

sections.title: Paid Care Work
sections.big_idea: Paid care is a largely female, largely informal workforce with a wage discount. **Its pay is a public-finance question.**
in_plain_words: Paid care covers domestic workers, nurses, teachers, childcare and eldercare staff and frontline ASHAs and anganwadi workers. Most sit outside formal employment, so minimum wage and social security do not reach them. The classification is the policy: employee, volunteer or self-employed decides what follows. Domestic work is hard to regulate because the workplace is a home, though organising has worked.

The care penalty is a wage discount that persists after skill and education, and applies to men in care jobs too. It persists because care is seen as natural, quality is hard to measure, work is informal and users cannot pay much. Decent work has five elements, and registration is the first practical step. **Better pay is a double dividend** for workers and for the quality of care.

key_terms.meaning: The wage discount on care jobs after accounting for skill and education.
The ILO Domestic Workers Convention.
Community health worker classed as a volunteer paid on incentives.
Child development worker paid an honorarium.
Fair wages, protection, safety, reasonable hours and the right to organise.
Benefit of care that reaches people who do not pay for it.

worked_example.title: Measure a care penalty
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. Comparable work for the same skill and education pays Rs 12,000 a month, and the care job pays Rs 9,000.
steps: Penalty as a share of the comparison wage: 3,000 ÷ 12,000 = 0.25.
So the care job carries a 25% discount in this example.
Check the third row of the deck's table: if men in the same care job also earn less, the penalty attaches to the occupation.
Explain it by spillover benefits: users and society gain without paying.
worked_example.answer: A 25% wage discount (illustrative), which is a care penalty if skill and education are matched.

mistakes: Expecting care wages to rise through market pressure when users cannot pay.
Treating honoraria as pay for full-time required work.
Skipping registration, so workers cannot be reached by other protections.
Calling the penalty a gender gap alone, when it also affects men in care jobs.

recall.q: What is the care penalty?
recall.a: The wage discount attached to care jobs after accounting for skill and education.

recall.q: What is the status of ASHAs and anganwadi workers?
recall.a: ASHAs are volunteers on task-based incentives and anganwadi workers receive an honorarium.

recall.q: Why is domestic work hard to regulate?
recall.a: The workplace is a private home, the employer a household, hours can be live-in and workers are isolated.

recall.q: What is the first practical step for decent work?
recall.a: Registration.

recall.q: What is the second dividend of better care pay?
recall.a: Better quality of care for children, patients and elders.

sections.title: Care in South Asia
sections.big_idea: Rising care demand meets falling supply and a mostly informal economy. **Design for the informal majority.**
in_plain_words: South Asia combines a very wide unpaid-care gender gap, low female labour-force participation, thin public services, high informality and rapid demographic change. These interact. Joint families are giving way to nuclear households, adults migrate, and ageing raises the demand for eldercare. A care crisis opens where demand rises and supply falls, and the default answer is more unpaid work for women.

Informality shapes everything, so entitlements tied to formal employment reach a small minority of working women. Universal or residence-based provision is the design response. The paradox that education and incomes rose while participation stayed low points to the care burden. Worksite crèches, community kitchens and water and LPG schemes exist. **The task is to fund, connect and scale them.**

key_terms.meaning: The gap between rising care demand and falling supply.
A migrating carer's own care needs are filled by another woman further down.
Work outside formal employment, beyond leave laws and social security.
A household where adults migrated, leaving care and farm work to women.
Entitlement through residence and citizenship, with no job required.
Spending that creates care jobs and frees other women to work.

worked_example.title: Will this entitlement reach informal women?
worked_example.setup: A state proposes a leave entitlement for employees with a contract and social security registration.
steps: Ask: does an informal woman have an employer of record? Usually no.
Ask: does she have a contract or social security registration? Usually no.
So the entitlement excludes the informal majority of working women.
The design response is universal or residence-based provision.
Note the cost: more expensive per head, and it reaches those employment-linked schemes cannot.
worked_example.answer: It misses most working women. A residence-based version would reach them at a higher cost per head.

mistakes: Designing policy for the formal minority, like 26-week leave alone.
Treating a higher participation rate as better work without checking its composition.
Counting the care that shifts to left-behind women as no migration effect.
Waiting to build eldercare, which takes a decade, while the transition is under way.

recall.q: What is the defining feature of South Asian care?
recall.a: Informality.

recall.q: What is a care crisis?
recall.a: The gap between rising care demand and falling supply.

recall.q: What is the care paradox?
recall.a: Women's education and household incomes have risen, yet female labour-force participation stayed low or fell.

recall.q: What did the recent uptick in participation largely consist of?
recall.a: Rural self-employment.

recall.q: Name two bright spots in the region.
recall.a: Any two of: SEWA and SHGs, worksite crèches, community kitchens and school meals, water and LPG schemes.

sections.title: Practice & Policy
sections.big_idea: Care investment pays twice, but only with jobs for the time released. **Cost the unpaid time your design assumes.**
in_plain_words: The closing case is that investing in care is one of the highest-return, most equitable investments an economy can make. Childcare returns to children, mothers and care workers, eldercare to elders and family carers, water and fuel to every household member's time, and care worker pay to the quality of care. Immediate effects are what a finance ministry can verify, and the longer-run ones justify the scale.

For practitioners: count care in baselines, check whose unpaid time your programme assumes, treat water, fuel and childcare as in scope, pay care workers and schedule around care. For policy: fund ECCE and anganwadis, extend leave to informal workers, build eldercare early, formalise and pay the care workforce, and invest in water, fuel and sanitation. **Every item maps to an R.**

key_terms.meaning: Care jobs created plus other women freed to work.
Healthier, better-raised, better-educated future workers.
An assumed price used to make unpaid time visible in a budget.
Relying on women's unpaid time that no budget records.
The five policy asks, each mapped to an R.
The criterion for choosing which R to push first.

worked_example.title: Cost the unpaid time
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A programme needs 200 hours of women's time over the project and you use a notional rate of Rs 50 an hour.
steps: Name the input: 200 hours of women's unpaid time.
Notional value: 200 × 50 = 10,000 rupees.
Add it to the budget as an input, even though no cash changes hands.
Ask whether the 200 hours should be reduced (infrastructure), redistributed or paid.
Show the line to everyone reviewing the design.
worked_example.answer: A Rs 10,000 notional input (illustrative) that is now visible. That visibility is the first R.

mistakes: Assuming care spending pays back without jobs for the time released.
Engaging 'volunteers' when the work is care that should be paid.
Pushing all five Rs at once when only one has a measurable near-term effect.
Leaving water and sanitation out of care policy.

recall.q: What does 'double dividend' mean?
recall.a: Care jobs created plus other women freed to work.

recall.q: Which practice step most changes designs?
recall.a: Do not free-ride: cost the unpaid time your design assumes.

recall.q: Which R does 'invest in water, fuel and transport' map to?
recall.a: Reduce.

recall.q: What does the deck suggest if you can push only one R?
recall.a: The one with a measurable near-term effect; Recognition first if nothing is measured, otherwise reduction.

recall.q: Which takeaway does the deck say to keep if you keep one?
recall.a: The third: care falls on women and girls, so ask whose time you are spending.

notes.2: Read the agenda as a three-part route. Sections 1 to 4 teach you to see, count and value care, sections 5 and 6 explain who carries it and why the economy depends on it, and sections 7 to 11 turn that into the 5 Rs, policies, paid work, the region and practice. If time is short, **start with section 7**.
notes.4: Hold the definition and the table together. Paid and unpaid care, direct and indirect, form one system that sustains people. The last row is where categories break: ASHAs are called volunteers, paid an honorarium and relied on by the health system. The slide says **classifying the work as voluntary is what makes it affordable**.
notes.5: Read the table down each column and then across. Unpaid care is done overwhelmingly by women and girls, and paid care is also done overwhelmingly by women, at pay below comparable work. The pattern is one thing seen on both sides of the household boundary, which is **the core claim of care economics**.
notes.6: Separate direct care from the housework that makes it possible. The bottom two rows of the table are where policy has most traction, since cooking and water can be reduced by services and infrastructure. Watch supervision: **hours of being available** are a real constraint, and instruments capture them badly.
notes.7: Trace the circuit once with your finger: care produces people, people supply labour, markets generate output, and output funds services and care. When public services contract, the load returns to households and then to women. That is why **austerity has a gendered incidence** even when the budget lines cut look gender-neutral.
notes.8: Use these as established global estimates and cite them with source and year: 16.4 billion hours a day, 76% done by women, equal to 2 billion people working 8 hours unpaid. The slide warns that estimates vary by method, so **quote the basis with the number** to avoid a methodological dismissal.
notes.9: Learn to make the argument in finance-ministry language. Conventional accounting books childcare, maternity benefit, eldercare and water infrastructure as cost, while the care lens books them as investment. The classification changes appraisal and how easily a line is cut, so **make the case as human-capital investment** where you can.
notes.10: Use the working day to test your programme. Every item before 'work' begins is displaced by infrastructure or shared with another person, and none of it by exhortation, which is why Reduce and Redistribute are separate Rs. If you ask for two hours a week, **ask what those hours compete with**: sleep, paid work or a daughter's schooling.
notes.11: Treat the roadmap as two halves: seeing and measuring, then acting on it. Pick your starting point by role. An analyst should read sections 2 to 4 closely, a programme designer sections 5 to 8, and a policy adviser sections 7, 8 and 11. **Examples are India-centric** throughout.
notes.13: Remember the pairs: a meal at home against a meal in a restaurant, the same work with a different price tag. The boundary follows whether money changed hands, which is a measurement convention and no economic judgement. One consequence is perverse: **as services commercialise, GDP rises** without new work being done.
notes.14: Learn the asymmetry in the first two rows: growing food for your own household counts as production, while cooking it does not. The SNA includes own-use production of goods and excludes unpaid services. The defence is that goods are countable and household services are hard to count, a defence **time-use surveys have weakened considerably**.
notes.15: Use the housekeeper paradox as a conversation starter. The same work counts as production when paid and as nothing when unpaid, so GDP moves when work crosses the household line. The slide's conclusion is the one to use: GDP is **a poor measure of how much work is being done**.
notes.16: Explain how care became 'not work': it was naturalised as love and instinct, so no skill, ladder or pay followed. The last row is the operational one for practitioners: programme designs that assume women will contribute unpaid time **rely on this framing to work**. The same framing produces the care penalty in paid care.
notes.17: Link each thinker to one idea: Waring and the SNA, Folbre and the care penalty, Elson and the Rs, Razavi and the care diamond, Hochschild and the second shift. You will meet each again. Elson's three Rs are **the most policy-portable output** and now sit in mainstream language with the ILO's two additions.
notes.18: Read the right-hand column as a list of design defects. A programme that treats care as free gives it no budget line, targets women as 'not working', schedules activities they cannot attend and adds to their load unnoticed. The cheapest correction on the slide: **add two time-use questions to a baseline**.
notes.19: Treat the chart as an illustration patterned on time-use estimates, with no real figures. The message is that a large share of socially useful work is unpaid care that never enters GDP. Estimates vary by method, and **every serious one puts a large share below the waterline**.
notes.20: Notice the compromise: satellite accounts value household production alongside GDP without changing the headline number. For advocacy that is usually enough, because it gives you an official figure to cite. Time-use surveys are the raw material, and India has had **2019 and 2024 rounds**.
notes.22: Know what a time-use survey sees that other surveys miss: the full 24 hours, unpaid work by activity, simultaneous activities, who in the household, and weekday and weekend variation. The third row is where care is most often lost. Check whether a figure counts secondary activity, because that **roughly doubles the care total**.
notes.23: Cite the round whenever you use a figure. India's first national TUS covered January to December 2019, a second round was released in February 2025, and two rounds five years apart make change measurable for the first time. Compare them only after reading how the **instrument changed**.
notes.24: Follow the four steps and then focus on the weak point: who is interviewed. Proxy reporting is the largest hazard, since one person reporting for the household gives the norm and misses the day. Read departures from individual recall as **likely to understate women's hours**.
notes.25: Treat the numbers on the slide as illustrative. What is well established is that Indian women spend many times more of their day than men on unpaid domestic and care work. Use the last row in design: **a large unpaid-care load decides which women an eleven o'clock activity reaches**.
notes.26: Look at the bars as a pattern only. The key point sits below the chart: the gap holds across rural and urban settings and across states, which suggests a norm and no artefact of one region. So **redistribution needs norm work as well as services**. The size varies and the direction does not.
notes.27: Use time-use data to size the problem and target policy, and read it like any survey. It shows how much care is done and by whom, captures simultaneous work and supports satellite accounts. It cannot explain why the division exists or capture the mental load, so **read a reported gap as a lower bound**.
notes.28: Remember the infrastructure table: no piped water, no LPG, no electricity and no sanitation each add hours for women while men's hours barely move. That is why the division looks like a norm. It also identifies the highest-return interventions: **infrastructure reduces the total, and only redistribution changes the share**.
notes.29: Use the table to see why a national round matters at design. Time-use evidence supports childcare investment, leave design, infrastructure priorities, satellite accounts and programme timing, and none of it requires new data once a round exists. **Read the TUS tables for your own state** before designing an activity schedule.
notes.31: Learn imputation as a chain of choices: which activities, whose wage, whether to value simultaneous time and whether to include supervision. Each choice moves the total, so published estimates for one country legitimately range widely. **Report the method and prefer a range** to a single confident figure.
notes.32: Use the table to ask which method any figure uses. Generalist replacement cost gives the lower estimate, specialist replacement a higher one, and opportunity cost varies with the carer's wage. Opportunity cost has the uncomfortable property of valuing a well-paid woman's hour above a poor one's, so **most official exercises use generalist replacement**.
notes.33: Quote the range with its drivers: valuations typically land between roughly 10% and 60% of GDP depending on method and country. The slide's last line is the key: the spread **follows arithmetically from method choices** and reflects no disagreement about the facts. The chart is illustrative.
notes.34: Use the comparison to named sectors carefully. It makes an abstract share concrete and reaches finance audiences, but a sceptical economist will ask about the method. The slide reminds you that the purpose is recognition: **nothing follows from 'bigger than manufacturing'** unless a policy decision hangs on it.
notes.35: Keep these four aims as your reasons to monetise: reach ministries that speak in money, justify investment in childcare, eldercare and leave, show the scale of women's contribution, and track whether burdens rise or are shared. Pair this slide with the next one on limits, because **valuation helps and carries risk**.
notes.36: Notice the circularity risk: valuing unpaid care at a domestic worker's wage prices it at a rate that is itself depressed because the work is coded as care. A price also invites cost-cutting. Use valuation to win recognition and budget, and **keep the hours and the distribution in view**.
notes.37: Take the balance as a working rule. Care is an economic activity worth measuring and a relationship that resists being priced, and you hold both. Use valuation to win recognition and resources while insisting that **care's worth exceeds its monetary estimate**.
notes.39: Remember the headline: women spend 3.2 times as much time on unpaid care as men worldwide, from 1.7 times in the Americas to 4.7 times in the Arab States. The table shows each institution assuming the others enforce the pattern. So **single-point interventions disappoint**, while a crèche plus school timings plus transport plus shared leave changes the day.
notes.40: Link childhood to later outcomes. Girls drawn into fetching, cooking and sibling care lose study time and risk dropout, while boys who are exempted never acquire care skills or habits. Programmes that engage boys in care tasks work on **supply for the next generation**, slowly, and it is one of the few things that shifts the norm.
notes.41: Define time poverty precisely: too little time left for rest, learning, paid work or leisure after unavoidable unpaid work. A person can be income-poor and time-poor together, and the two respond to different interventions. Measuring it needs a **stated threshold**, because how much discretionary time counts as enough is a judgement.
notes.42: Remember Hochschild's finding: paid work adds to the day and replaces none of it. Cooking, childcare, elder care and the mental load stay hers, and sleep and leisure are squeezed. That is the strongest argument for pairing Reduce and Redistribute, since **more paid work without less care gives a longer day**.
notes.43: Read the chart as an illustration of a relationship: the heavier the unpaid-care load, the lower female labour-force participation. The table limits the claim, since it shows association and leaves open which causes which. The policy reading survives that: **reducing and redistributing care relaxes the constraint** whichever direction dominates.
notes.44: Use the intersection table to see the range behind the average. Poverty, rurality, caste, disability in the household and adult migration each add to the load. Disaggregate care data by **at least two axes** wherever the sample allows: the mean shows the gap exists and the crossing shows where to act.
notes.45: Add the mental load to your picture: planning, remembering and worrying never occupy a diary slot, so time-use data cannot see them. The load also fails to redistribute when tasks do. A man who cooks on request while a woman decides what is cooked has **shared the task and left the load**.
notes.46: Use the table to answer the charge that the claim is ideological. Each consequence of the unequal load can be evidenced from public Indian data: PLFS with TUS, household surveys, time-use and health data, asset and account data. Redistribution has the largest potential effect, because it **changes the share and the total stays put**.
notes.48: Hold social reproduction as a dependency visible in both directions: markets rely on care for workers, and care relies on the incomes markets provide. The table shows households, mostly women, absorbing daily, generational, illness and community care, with **no payment from the market at any point** in the cycle.
notes.49: Treat depletion as an account that can run down. Care extracted without replenishment shows up in health, exhaustion, withdrawal from paid work and care quality. The practical warning is on the last line: a new committee, form or meeting for carers **draws on this account**. Count the extra demand before you add it.
notes.50: Use the reframing for budgets: spending on childcare, health and eldercare is booked as consumption to contain, while care builds human capital. The classification decides which appraisal method applies and whether long-run returns can be counted. **Care as social infrastructure** is the argument that moves it across the line.
notes.51: Learn the diamond: state, market, family and community provide care. When the first two do little, the family corner, in practice women, absorbs the rest. The framework makes the split between corners **a visible policy choice**, which a society can no longer treat as a fixed fact.
notes.52: Use the examples to audit each corner: anganwadis and ASHAs (limit: coverage and quality), crèches and private nurses (affordability), mothers and daughters-in-law (depletion), SHGs and neighbours (fragile). Community provision is often credited as a solution, so **check who is doing it** before crediting it. Usually it is unpaid women's work.
notes.53: Treat the diamond as a lever: shifting care toward the state needs public spending and staffing, toward the market needs affordability or subsidy, toward men needs norm change and leave design, and toward the community needs payment. **Name which corner you are shifting care to, and who pays**; that is the substance of a care policy.
notes.54: Use the multiplier for macro audiences. Care services are labour-intensive, so spending creates many jobs per rupee, mostly for women, and frees other women to work. The last row matters most in a macro argument: care spending has low import content, so it **stays in the domestic economy** far more than capital-intensive alternatives.
notes.56: Learn the 5 Rs by origin: Elson's three (Recognise, Reduce, Redistribute) and the ILO's two (Represent, Reward). Treat them as a set. Reduce without Redistribute lowers the total and leaves the share unchanged, and Recognise alone **produces a report**. Each R has a hardest part, shown in the table.
notes.57: Use the second table for audits. Each R has a typical instrument and a characteristic nominal version: measured then shelved, hours released with the share unchanged, norms untouched, consultation without authority, honoraria instead of pay. The clearest test across all five is money: **which Rs have a budget line and how large is it**.
notes.58: Treat Recognise as the precondition, and see that it is only the start. A country can measure care in great detail and redistribute none of it. For a practitioner the third row is the one you control: **two time-use questions in your own baseline** make the care load in your programme area visible.
notes.59: Use Reduce when you need quick, evidenced results. Piped water, LPG, electricity, sanitation and transport return hours and work through capital investment. Jal Jeevan and Ujjwala are in effect care-reduction policies. The limit is that released hours can be absorbed by other unpaid work, so **check where the hours go**.
notes.60: Face the hardest R directly. Redistribute moves care from women to men and from families to the state and market, and it confronts norms head-on. The best-evidenced instrument is non-transferable leave, because take-up rises when the entitlement is lost if unused. Redistribute comes last and gets least funding because **it requires someone to do more**.
notes.61: Represent makes the other Rs durable, because it creates a constituency that will defend a care budget line under pressure. The examples are domestic-worker unions and ASHA and anganwadi collectives. The omitted row is care users' voice: policy is written about elders and disabled people **far more often than with them**.
notes.62: Reward closes the loop. Decent wages, social protection, safe conditions and recognition of skill answer the care penalty directly. The first row is a live dispute in India, where frontline workers doing sustained, required work are classed as volunteers on an honorarium. Check whether your programme's workers are **paid or merely thanked**.
notes.63: Use the sequence to see dependencies. Recognition comes first and the rest depend on it, reduction is cheaper than redistribution, and reward without representation rarely sticks. Most national care policies stop after the second R, so measured burdens fall slowly while **the gender share barely moves**.
notes.64: Run the five questions at your next design meeting: ten minutes is enough. The failing answers show what to listen for, such as 'we ask about employment' or 'volunteers'. Most designs fail the third question, and **failing it is what makes the others academic**.
notes.66: Map every instrument to an R. Childcare serves Redistribute, water and fuel serve Reduce, leave serves Redistribute, wages serve Reward and time-use serves Recognise. Most national policies cluster in one or two Rs, and **the gaps are usually Represent and Reward**. Income support spans several.
notes.67: Check the hours condition first. ECCE does double duty only when quality and staffing are adequate and hours match a working day. A centre open for three hours does not enable paid work, however good it is for the child. NEP 2020 is an opening, and **delivery stays a question of anganwadi capacity**.
notes.68: Cost the anganwadi worker's day. ICDS offers nutrition, pre-school and health services through about 14 lakh centres, with a growing reporting burden, usually for an honorarium. Any proposal to expand what anganwadis deliver adds to that person's day, so **say so and cost it** or the expansion is unfunded by design.
notes.69: Spot the two gaps that compound: the 26 weeks of paid maternity leave cover mainly the formal sector, a small minority of working women, and the entitlement attaches to mothers, so it does not redistribute. The design question on the slide is **whether the entitlement follows the job or the person**.
notes.70: Treat eldercare as the care crisis arriving fastest, because the demographic change is already determined and the provision is almost entirely familial. It falls on women twice, as carers and as the majority of the very old, who are more likely to be widowed and **without income**.
notes.71: Read the social protection budget as care policy. Pensions, maternity benefit, disability support and child grants put resources behind carers and the people they care for, and most budgets label none of them care policy. The exercise **usually reveals more care spending than the care line does**, and more gaps.
notes.72: Take the direction and leave the template. The Nordic systems were built over decades with a tax base few developing economies have. The transferable point is the second row: **making part of leave non-transferable** is a low-cost design change with well-documented effects on the within-household share.
notes.73: Use the four questions to read any policy. The third decides in South Asia, because entitlements tied to formal employment reach a small minority of working women. The fourth is the free-riding test: a policy delivered by volunteers or honorarium workers **transfers cost instead of funding care**.
notes.75: Look at who the paid workforce is: domestic workers, ASHAs, anganwadi workers, nurses and private crèche staff. Most sit outside formal employment, which means outside minimum wage, social security and enforcement. The slide puts it well: **the classification is the policy**, since employee, volunteer or self-employed determines everything after.
notes.76: Understand why domestic work is hard to regulate: a private home as workplace, a household as employer, live-in hours and isolation. C189 sets standards, but ratification and enforcement remain limited. Organising has worked where it was sustained, and **SEWA and domestic-worker unions** are the clearest South Asian examples.
notes.77: Learn the three statuses: ASHAs as volunteers on task-based incentives, anganwadi workers on honoraria, ANMs usually salaried. Their status has been the subject of collective action and litigation. The practical point is narrow: **any programme routed through them adds to a day that is already full** and often unpaid.
notes.78: Define the care penalty as the wage discount on care jobs after accounting for skill and education. The third row is the strongest evidence that it attaches to the occupation, since men in care jobs earn less than comparable men elsewhere. Folbre explains it by **spillover benefits** that people who do not pay still receive.
notes.79: Read this table as a list of changeable choices: certification, standards, organising and public funding. The fourth row is decisive, because those who need care most are least able to pay. That makes care wages **a public-finance question** and a labour-market one only secondarily, which is where the argument has to be made.
notes.80: Use the decent work elements as an audit of any care programme: fair wages, social protection, safety, reasonable hours and the right to organise. Each has a hard version in care. Start with registration, because **a worker who is recorded nowhere cannot be reached** by any of the other four.
notes.81: Treat the chart as an illustration of the care penalty: paid care occupations cluster below average earnings, domestic work near the bottom and frontline health and nutrition below wage floors. Because users cannot pay more, the **level is set by public funding** and demand has little say.
notes.82: Use the double dividend in your pitch to service ministries. Better pay lifts a large female workforce out of precarity and improves the quality of care for children, patients and elders. Turnover is the measurable link, so **make the case in continuity and training cost** where you can.
notes.84: Read the five features together: a very wide unpaid-care gap, low female labour-force participation, thin public services, high informality and rapid demographic change. They interact. Because thin services and informality close off both state and employer, South Asian care policy must reach people **through residence and citizenship** and employment alone will miss most women.
notes.85: Follow three shifts: nuclearisation leaves fewer hands, male out-migration moves care and farm work to women who stay, and female migration creates care chains. The care that shifts to left-behind women is rarely counted as a **migration effect**. Ask who fills the gap when someone leaves.
notes.86: See the care crisis as the gap between rising demand and falling supply. The question is only who absorbs it, and historically it has been women, at the cost of their participation and health. The alternatives need a decision, while **the default requires none**.
notes.87: Plan for ageing now. The share of people aged 60+ is projected to roughly double, and pensions and services are thin, so demand lands first on families and women. The workforce is the binding constraint: **training and paying eldercare workers** has the longest lead time.
notes.88: Use the window: the child population is large now and will shrink. Anganwadis upgraded into full ECCE centres could support child development and women's employment together, provided hours match a working day. Infrastructure built for the young can **later serve eldercare demand**.
notes.89: Design for the informal majority. No employer of record, no contract, no social security registration and no inspection each exclude women from maternity benefit, leave, pensions and enforcement. The design response is **universal or residence-based provision**, which costs more per head and reaches those employment-linked schemes miss.
notes.90: Treat the paradox as a puzzle with several explanations, the unequal and unsupported care burden among the strongest. Growth alone has not freed women's time. Read the recent uptick in participation carefully: it is largely rural self-employment, and **a higher rate is not automatically better work**.
notes.91: Collect the bright spots as building blocks: SEWA and SHG federations, worksite crèches, community kitchens and school meals, and Jal Jeevan and Ujjwala. The crèche examples matter because they solve the hours problem. The slide says the gap is **funding and coverage**, since each model already works at scale somewhere.
notes.93: Use the closing case with its caveat. Investing in care pays twice, through the service and through the time and earnings it releases, and it builds human capital. The returns depend on jobs existing for the time released, so **pair care investment with a jobs policy**.
notes.94: Read the chart as an illustration of direction: because care is labour-intensive, a rupee invested in care typically creates more jobs, many for women, than the same rupee in construction. Cite the ILO studies it is patterned on, and **treat the bars themselves as illustrative**.
notes.95: Read the two columns together when making a budget case. The immediate effects are what a finance ministry can verify, and the longer-run ones justify the scale. Water and sanitation are rarely presented as care policy yet are **among the largest hour-returning investments** available.
notes.96: Turn the five practice steps into project rules. The second changes designs most: if your programme needs 200 hours of women's time, that is a 200-hour input missing from the budget. Write it in even at a notional rate, and **pay care workers instead of 'engaging volunteers'**.
notes.97: Map each policy ask to an R. Most national care policies concentrate on Reduce and on services for children, and stop. If you can push only one, push the one with a measurable near-term effect in your context: **Recognition first if nothing is measured**, otherwise reduction.
notes.98: Choose a reading by role. Folbre for the economics of care, Elson for the Rs, ILO 2018 for the global numbers and Razavi for the diamond. The slide also names three ImpactMojo companion courses. Start with **the ILO report** if you need figures to cite.
notes.99: Take the five takeaways as five questions you can ask in any design meeting without preparation. If you keep one, keep the third: almost every unexamined assumption in development programming resolves into **unpaid women's time**.
